Monday: Arnab's history project was due on Friday. At nine he lay on his bed with his phone. "Tomorrow I'll be fresh," he told his sister Kalyani when she asked. "Tuesday me is way more serious." He watched videos until midnight.
Wednesday: Tuesday had gone the same way. Now he scrolled with a small knot in his stomach, the empty project file open on the laptop behind the phone. "Tomorrow, full focus," he muttered. Kalyani raised an eyebrow and said nothing.
Friday, 6 a.m.: Arnab sat at the dining table, eyes red, gluing pictures onto chart paper and scribbling captions. He handed it in half-finished. That evening he asked Kalyani to keep his phone until eight.

qa.a: Arnab's history project was due on Friday.

qa.q: Why did 'Tuesday me is way more serious' feel true to Arnab on Monday night?
qa.a: Tonight he felt tired and the videos were easy, so he imagined a fresher, more serious self tomorrow who would happily do the hard part.

qa.q: What turning point does Arnab reach, and why might it help?
qa.a: He asks Kalyani to keep his phone until eight, which removes the scrolling at the moment he usually gives in instead of trusting tomorrow's mood.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Arnab hands her the phone on Friday evening?
qa.a: She may feel quietly glad, having watched the week unfold without lecturing, and pleased he chose the fix himself.

passage:
Sit, Sonali. You say you'll study tomorrow? Then let your Mehak Nani tell you about your Pradeep Mama when he was fifteen.
Every night he told me, "Ma, tomorrow I'll wake at five and finish algebra. Tonight I'm too tired." Then he sat on the terrace turning the pages of film magazines till eleven. In the morning? "Tonight, Ma, I'll feel more like it."
He truly believed the Pradeep of tomorrow would be a different boy, stronger. I watched this for a month. Then the half-yearly results came, and he cried on this same step.
After that, he did one small page each night before the magazines. Just one.
Tomorrow is a nice place, beta, but nobody lives there.

qa.q: What did Pradeep read on the terrace at night?
qa.a: He turned the pages of film magazines till eleven.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep keep believing tomorrow would be better?
qa.a: Each night he felt too tired, and he pictured a stronger Pradeep who would wake at five, so putting it off felt sensible, not lazy.

qa.q: What choice finally changed things for Pradeep?
qa.a: Doing one small page each night before the magazines, a task so small that tonight's tired self could still manage it.

qa.q: Why might Mehak Nani tell this story to Sonali instead of just scolding?
qa.a: Nani hopes Sonali will see the same pattern in the story of a beloved uncle and feel understood rather than judged.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage son who always promised to study the next day, trusting that he would feel more willing then.

Uday's maths test was on Thursday, and his cousin Pallavi, the only one at home who understood trigonometry, was leaving for her hostel on Wednesday morning.
"Sit with me tonight," she offered on Monday.
"Tomorrow," Uday said, thumb flicking through short videos. "I'll feel sharper tomorrow."
On Tuesday a power cut hit at seven. When the fans spun again at ten, Uday was still scrolling. "Tomorrow morning, early," he told her.
On Wednesday at six, Pallavi's bag was by the door and the auto was honking. Uday ran out with his notebook. "Just one sum?"
She laughed tiredly and worked one sum with him on the auto step.

qa.q: What happened on Tuesday at seven?
qa.a: A power cut hit at seven.

qa.q: What did Uday expect to feel 'tomorrow', and why did that seem believable to him?
qa.a: He expected to feel sharper, because tonight he was comfortable scrolling and assumed a future Uday would be more in the mood for trigonometry.

qa.q: At which point could Uday have made a better choice, and what?
qa.a: On Monday, when Pallavi offered, he could have put the phone away and sat with her for even half an hour, since her help had a clear end date.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel working one sum on the auto step?
qa.a: She seems tired and a bit exasperated, yet still kind enough to help in her last minute, perhaps wishing he had come on Monday.

"Weren't you going to do the first three chapters today?" his sister Disha asked.
"Tomorrow. Tomorrow I'll wake up fresh. Wednesday me is way more focused."

She raised an eyebrow. "Every day you say tomorrow you'll feel like it."

"Parth, it's nine. What happened to the geography map?"
"Tomorrow, Mummy. I'll do it in the morning before school."
"You said that yesterday."
"Yesterday I was tired. Tomorrow I'll be fresh."
Mehak put the dal on the table. "Sonali, what time did he get up today?"
"Seven fifty," Sonali said, grinning. "He ran to the bus with toast in his mouth."
"That was a one-time thing, didi."
"It's been a one-time thing every day this week."
Parth looked at the empty map lying on the chair. "Okay, but tomorrow morning will be different. I can feel it."
Mehak sat down. "What will be different about tomorrow's you?"
He opened his mouth, closed it, and reached for his phone.

passage: Every evening in Kollengode, after cricket on the temple ground, Madhav told his sister Gopika the same thing: "Hindi essay tomorrow, first thing, before school." The essay was due on Friday. On Monday, tomorrow seemed perfect: he'd be fresh, the house would be quiet. On Tuesday morning he overslept. Tuesday evening there was a match against the next village, so Wednesday for sure. On Wednesday night the power went out, which felt like proof he couldn't. On Thursday at ten at night, Madhav sat under the tube light with a blank page while Gopika read nearby. "Why didn't you do it on Monday?" she asked. Madhav opened his mouth. On Monday, Tuesday's Madhav had seemed like a better person. He picked up the pen.

qa.q: When was the Hindi essay due?
qa.a: The essay was due on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Madhav keep saying 'tomorrow'?
qa.a: Madhav felt relaxed after cricket and sure that the next morning's self would be fresh and willing, so putting it off felt reasonable each time.

qa.q: What could Madhav do differently with the next essay?
qa.a: Start a small piece the same evening, even ten minutes after cricket, instead of trusting a 'first thing tomorrow' plan.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Madhav's Thursday night?
qa.a: Gopika probably finds it predictable, having heard 'tomorrow' every evening, and asks gently why he didn't start on Monday.

grounding: Shows a teenager promising each night to write an essay tomorrow and ending up with a blank page the night before.

passage: In Abuja, Emeka had eight weeks to write the essay for a science boarding-school scholarship. "I work best under pressure," he told his cousin Lindiwe, visiting from Johannesburg. Every night he opened the document, typed a title, and reached for his phone. One video. Then another. Tomorrow he would feel more inspired; tonight he was tired from football. Lindiwe watched this for a week. On Saturday she sat beside him and pointed at the calendar. "Seven weeks now. Tomorrow-you is exactly the same as you, only with less time." Emeka laughed, then stopped. He wrote one paragraph that night, badly. The next night, two. By the end of the month there was a draft, and he admitted the pressure had never once helped.

qa.q: How many weeks did Emeka have for the essay at first?
qa.a: He had eight weeks.

qa.q: Why did Emeka keep reaching for his phone and saying tomorrow would be better?
qa.a: Emeka felt tired from football and sure that a future, more inspired self would do the work, so tonight's videos felt harmless.

qa.q: What changed when Emeka started writing one paragraph a night?
qa.a: The work became small enough to start now, so it no longer depended on a future mood, and a draft appeared by the end of the month.

qa.q: How did Lindiwe see Emeka's 'I work best under pressure'?
qa.a: Lindiwe saw a pattern of delay and reminded him that tomorrow's Emeka is the same person with less time.

grounding: Shows a teenager postponing an essay night after night, sure his future self will feel more like working.

passage: Study hour in the boys' hostel at the Dehradun school ran from seven to nine. Asif had a chemistry test on Thursday. On Monday, he opened his book, then his phone. "I'll start properly tomorrow," he told his roommate Hemant. "Tomorrow I'll be fresh." He scrolled until the warden's bell. On Tuesday, the same. "Tomorrow for sure. I'll do double." On Wednesday night he sat with four chapters and a cold feeling in his stomach. Hemant, who had done a chapter each night, watched him. "Tomorrow-Asif always sounds like a hero," Hemant said. "Tonight-Asif is the one who has to work." Asif laughed, but it hurt. The warden came by and suggested the phone stay in the locker during study hour from now on. Asif handed it over. He opened chapter one.

qa.a: From seven to nine.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling on Wednesday night?
qa.a: He felt anxious and regretful, with a cold feeling in his stomach, facing four chapters the night before the test.

qa.q: What did the warden suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Keeping the phone in the locker during study hour, which removes the temptation so tonight's Asif can start instead of waiting for tomorrow.

qa.a: Hemant sees them as heroic plans that never happen, since tomorrow-Asif never shows up.

Dear Imran bhai,
You told me to write to you when I'm stuck, so here I am.
Board exams are in six weeks. Every night I say, "Tomorrow I'll study six hours." Every night I scroll videos till one. And every morning I feel terrible, and then that night I say it again. It's like I'm sure tomorrow-me will feel like studying. But tomorrow-me is exactly the same as today-me. Same bed, same phone.
Ammi hasn't noticed yet. I'm scared she will.
You did your boards two years ago. How did you start? Not tomorrow. Today.
Please write back soon.
Your little brother,
Mridul

qa.q: How many weeks until Mridul's board exams?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What is Mridul feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: He feels scared and guilty, stuck in a loop of promising to study tomorrow and scrolling tonight.

qa.q: What could help Mridul start today rather than tomorrow?
qa.a: Asking Imran bhai for concrete tips, and starting with one small task tonight, like thirty minutes with the phone in another room.

qa.q: How might Imran bhai feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Imran bhai would probably feel concerned but also glad Mridul reached out for help.

Sachin, you say you'll start revising tomorrow? I said that for a whole year once. I'm your Lalit Chacha, so let me tell you about my Class 10.
Every evening I'd sit with my maths book, and every evening there was a cricket match on the colony ground, or a film on TV, or a friend at the gate. "Tomorrow I'll study four hours," I'd say. I truly believed tomorrow-Lalit would be a hero.
Tomorrow-Lalit was exactly like today-Lalit. He also liked cricket.
In February, with a month left, I panicked. My father didn't shout. He took a calendar and made me cross off the days I'd wasted. There were so many crosses the page looked black.
From that night I studied one hour first, every day, before any match. Only one. But it was today's hour, not tomorrow's.
I passed. Not brilliantly, but I passed.

qa.q: How many hours did Lalit promise to study 'tomorrow'?
qa.a: Lalit said, 'Tomorrow I'll study four hours.'

qa.q: Why did Lalit keep believing tomorrow would be different?
qa.a: Lalit felt hopeful and sure that tomorrow-Lalit would be a hero, while cricket and films felt irresistible today.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things, and why?
qa.a: Studying one hour first every day before any match, because it put the work in today instead of trusting tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Lalit's father have felt in February?
qa.a: The father was probably worried but calm, choosing to show the wasted days on a calendar instead of shouting.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a teenage habit of promising to study tomorrow, sure a future self would feel more like working.

The scholarship essay was due at midnight, and at 8 p.m. Bhupen hadn't written a word. For two weeks he had said, "Tomorrow, when I'm in the mood." The mood never came.
Now the wedding band next door was practising the same three songs, loud enough to rattle the windows, and the power kept flickering.
Siddharth messaged: "Done with yours?"
"Starting now," Bhupen typed.
"Bro. You said last Sunday."
"Last Sunday I was sure I'd feel more like it this week."
The lights went out. Bhupen sat in the dark with his phone at thirty percent, the band blaring, his heart racing.
"Okay," Siddharth wrote. "Write the first paragraph on your phone. Just five lines. Send them to me. I'll read."
Bhupen typed with his thumbs. Five lines. Then five more. The band switched songs. He didn't notice.

qa.a: The scholarship essay was due at midnight.

qa.q: Why had Bhupen waited two weeks to start?
qa.a: Bhupen felt hopeful that he would be more in the mood tomorrow, so starting today never felt necessary.

qa.a: Writing just five lines on the phone and sending them, which made starting small enough to do right away.
